body.text: iha khalu sākṣātparamparayā vā sarvān eva jīvān samuddidhīrṣur bhagavān śrīmacchaṅkaro 'nātmabhyo vivekenātmānaṃ nityaśuddhabuddhamuktasvabhāvaṃ saṃkṣepeṇa bodhayituṃ daśaślokīṃ praṇināya /
body.translated_text: Here indeed, the Blessed <s>Śrī Śaṅkara</s>, wishing to uplift all <s>jīvas</s> (individual souls) either directly or through a tradition of teachers, composed the <s>Daśaślokī</s> (Ten Verses) to briefly teach — through discrimination from the not-self — the <s>Ātman</s> (self), whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free.

body.text: nanv idaṅkārāspadebhyo 'nātmabhyo vivekenāhaṅkārāspadam ātmānaṃ sarvo loko 'ham asmīti pratyeti duḥkhaṃ cānubhavati / tena jñātajñāpakatvān niṣprayojanakatvāc ca ātmatattvapratipādanaṃ vyartham iti cet, na, cidbhāsyatvena lakṣaṇena idaṅkārāspadānām api dehendriyamanasāṃ pratibhāsato 'haṅkārāspadatvena tadavivekāt tena viśuddhe 'py ātmani duḥkhitvādyabhimānāt śāstrīyeṇaiva brahmatmaikyajñānena samūlasya tasya nivṛtteḥ / tasmād ajñātajñāpakatvāt saprayojanakatvāc cātmatattvapratipādanaṃ na vyartham /
body.translated_text: Objection: Everyone cognizes the self — which is the locus of the 'I'-notion (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>) — through discrimination from the not-self which is the locus of the 'this'-notion, thinking 'I am,' and also experiences suffering. Therefore, since it would be making known what is already known and would be purposeless, the teaching of the true nature of the self is futile. Reply: No, because the body, senses, and mind — though being loci of the 'this'-notion — appear as loci of the 'I'-notion by virtue of the characteristic of being illumined by consciousness (<s>cidbhāsyatva</s>); and because of non-discrimination from that [self], there is superimposition of suffering etc. even upon the pure self; and because the complete removal of that [superimposition] along with its root is through scriptural knowledge alone of the identity of <s>Brahman</s> and <s>Ātman</s>. Therefore, since it makes known what is not truly known and since it has a purpose, the teaching of the true nature of the self is not futile.

body.text: tasya cātmatattvasya "tattvam asi" (ChU VI.8.7) "ahaṃ brahmāsmi" (BAU I.4.10) ityādivedāntamahāvākyam eva pramāpakam / vākyaṃ ca padārthajñānadvāreṇaiva jñāpakam iti tattvampadārthayoḥ prakṛtavākyānukūlayor anyato 'siddhatvāt tāv api śāstreṇaiva pramātavyau yūpāhavanīyapadārthavat / tataś ca "yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante yena vā jātāni jīvanti" (TU III.1.1) ityādyāḥ sṛṣṭyādiśrutayas tatpadavācyārthasya samarpikāḥ "satyaṃ jñānam anantam" (TU II.1) ityādyās tu lakṣyārthasya / evaṃ jāgratsvapnasuṣuptyādiśrutayaḥ "tad yathā mahāmatsya ubhe kūle anusañcarati" (BAU IV.3.18) ityādyās tvampadavācyārthasya samarpikāḥ "yo 'yaṃ vijñānamayaḥ prāṇeṣu hṛdyantarjyotiḥ puruṣaḥ" (BAU IV.3.7) "na dṛṣṭer draṣṭāraṃ paśyeḥ" (BAU III.4.2) ityādyās tu lakṣyārthasya / tena prathamam avāntaravākyebhyo 'nubhūtayoḥ śuddhajīvabrahmaṇos tattvamasyādivākye mukhārthānvayānupapatter lakṣaṇayā smaraṇopapattiḥ / suṣuptau nirvikalpakasākṣicaitanyānubhavāṅgīkārāc ca advitīyabrahmajijjāpayiṣayā pravṛttānāṃ satyajñānādipadānām upādhiviśiṣṭacaitanye śaktatve 'pi caitanyamātre tātparyeṇa tatraiva tadaṃśe eva saṃskārodbodhāc ca / icchanti hi ākāśādipadād api nirvikalpakaṃ smaraṇaṃ tātparyādhīnatvāc chabdavṛtteḥ / etena pramitipramātror mahāvākyārthabodhe bhānam apāstam / asamprajñātasamādheḥ śrutismṛtisiddhatvāc ca / pārokṣyasadvitīyatvābhyāṃ ca na tattvampadārthamātrānubhavād eva kṛtakṛtyatā / vācyārthasya ca bhedāvabhāsān na paunaruktyam / lakṣyārthasya caikatvād akhaṇḍārthatā / padajanyasya ca smaraṇasya nirvikalpalavākyārthānukūlasya nirvikalpakatvam anubhavavad evāviruddham / savikalpakavākyārthabodhe ca savikalpakapadārthāpasthitir aṅgam / prakṛte ca nirvikalpako vākyārthabodhas tasyaiva pramātvenājñānanivartanasāmarthyāt / ato na lakṣyatāvacchedakam antareṇa lakṣaṇānupapattiḥ / prakṛtavākyārthānukūlapadārthopasthitir eva śaktilakṣaṇāsādhyatvāt /
body.translated_text: And the means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) for that reality of the self is the <s>Vedānta mahāvākya</s> (great sentence) alone, such as '<s>tat tvam asi</s>' ('You are That,' ChU VI.8.7) and '<s>ahaṃ brahmāsmi</s>' ('I am <s>Brahman</s>,' BAU I.4.10). And the sentence is the means of knowledge only through knowledge of the meanings of its constituent words. Since the meanings of the 'tat' (that) and 'tvam' (you) words that are favorable to the sentence under consideration are not established from any other source, those too must be ascertained through scripture alone — like the meanings of the terms '<s>yūpa</s>' (sacrificial post) and '<s>āhavanīya</s>' (fire). Therefore, the creation-related <s>śrutis</s> such as 'from which indeed these beings are born, by which once born they live' (TU III.1.1) etc. present the primary (<s>vācya</s>) meaning of the 'tat' word; while those such as '<s>satyaṃ jñānam anantam</s>' ('truth, knowledge, infinite,' TU II.1) etc. present its secondary (<s>lakṣya</s>) meaning. Similarly, the <s>śrutis</s> dealing with waking, dream, deep sleep, etc. such as 'just as a great fish moves along both banks' (BAU IV.3.18) etc. present the primary meaning of the 'tvam' word; while those such as 'this person made of intelligence among the vital breaths, the inner light in the heart' (BAU IV.3.7) and 'you cannot see the seer of sight' (BAU III.4.2) etc. present its secondary meaning. Therefore, first from subordinate sentences, the pure <s>jīva</s> and <s>Brahman</s> — as experienced — when the literal connection of their primary meanings in the sentence '<s>tat tvam asi</s>' etc. is impossible, are understood through secondary signification (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) by way of recollection. And because of the acceptance of the experience of attributeless witness-consciousness (<s>nirvikalpaka-sākṣi-caitanya</s>) in deep sleep, and because even though the words '<s>satya</s>' (truth), '<s>jñāna</s>' (knowledge), etc. — which have commenced with the intention of revealing non-dual <s>Brahman</s> — have the power to denote consciousness conditioned by <s>upādhis</s> (limiting adjuncts), their purport is in consciousness alone, and it is in that aspect alone that recollection is aroused. For they hold that even from words like '<s>ākāśa</s>' (space) etc., attributeless recollection [arises], since the function of words depends on purport (<s>tātparya</s>). By this, the appearance of the cognition and the cognizer in the meaning of the <s>mahāvākya</s> is set aside. And because <s>asamprajñāta samādhi</s> (non-cognitive absorption) is established by <s>śruti</s> and <s>smṛti</s>. And because of indirectness (<s>pārokṣya</s>) and having-a-second (<s>sadvitīyatva</s>), there is no fulfillment of purpose from the experience of the mere meanings of the 'tat' and 'tvam' words alone. And because the primary meaning involves the appearance of difference, there is no redundancy. And because of the oneness of the secondary meaning, there is partless meaning (<s>akhaṇḍārtha</s>). And the attributeless nature of the word-generated recollection, which is favorable to the attributeless sentence-meaning, is not contradictory, just like experience itself. In the qualified (<s>savikalpaka</s>) sentence-meaning cognition, the qualified word-meaning presentation is a subsidiary factor. And in the present case, the sentence-meaning cognition is attributeless, since it alone as the means of valid knowledge has the power to remove ignorance. Therefore, there is no impossibility of secondary signification without a delimiter of what is to be implied. The word-meaning presentation favorable to the present sentence-meaning is itself not achievable through [primary] denotative power or through [regular] indication.

body.text: nanu tarhi vedāntavākyebhya eva padārthopasthitau vākyārthabodhe ca sati tasya svata eva prāmāṇyāt tenājñānatatkāryanivṛttyanupapattau kiṃ vicāreṇeti cet, satyam, vedāntā yady api svataḥprāmāṇyān nirvikalpakam ātmasākṣātkāraṃ janayanti tathāpi mandamatīnāṃ vādivipratipattijasaṃśayapratibandhena tasyājñānanāśakatvāsāmarthyāt vicāreṇa tu saṃśayanivṛttau nirapavādam ajñānanivṛttir iti saṃśayabījabhūtavādivipratipattinirākaraṇārthaṃ vicāra ārabhyate /
body.translated_text: Objection: If from the <s>Vedānta</s> sentences themselves, when word-meanings are presented and sentence-meaning is cognized, that [cognition] is self-valid (<s>svataḥ prāmāṇya</s>), then since through it there would be removal of ignorance and its effects, what is the need for philosophical investigation (<s>vicāra</s>)? Reply: True, although the <s>Vedānta</s> texts, being self-valid, generate attributeless direct realization of the self, nevertheless, for those of dull intellect, due to the obstruction of doubt born from the conflicting views of disputants, that [realization] lacks the power to destroy ignorance. But through investigation, when doubt is removed, the removal of ignorance becomes unobstructed. Therefore, investigation is undertaken for the purpose of refuting the conflicting views of disputants, which are the seeds of doubt.

body.text: prathamo vibhāgaḥ /
body.translated_text: First Division

body.text: tvaṃpadārthanirṇayaḥ /
body.translated_text: Determination of the meaning of the 'tvam' (you) word

body.text: tatra tvampadārthe vipratipattayaḥ prathamaṃ pradarśyante / tatpadārthasya śāstratātparyaviṣayatayābhyarhitatve 'pi tvampadārthasya śāstraphalamokṣabhāgitayā tato 'py abhyarhitatvāt /
body.translated_text: Therein, the conflicting views regarding the meaning of the 'tvam' word are first presented. Although the meaning of the 'tat' word deserves priority as the subject of scriptural purport, the meaning of the 'tvam' word deserves even greater priority since it pertains to <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation), which is the fruit of scripture.

body.text: tatra dehākārapariṇatāni catvāri bhūtāny eva tvampadārtha iti cārvākāḥ / cakṣurādīni pratyekam ity apare / militānīty anye / mana ity eke / prāṇa ity anye / kṣaṇikaṃ vijñānam iti saugatāḥ / śūnyam iti mādhyamikāḥ / dehendriyātirikto dehaparimāṇa iti digambarāḥ / kartā bhoktā jaḍo vibhur iti vaiśeṣikatārkikaprābhākarāḥ / jaḍo bodhātmaka iti bhāṭṭāḥ / bhoktaiva kevalabodhātmaka iti sāṅkhyāḥ pātañjalāś ca / avidyayā kartṛtvādibhāk paramārthato nirdharmakaḥ paramānandabodharūpa evety aupaniṣadāḥ / evaṃ sāmānyato 'hampratyayasiddhacidātmani vādivipratipattibhiḥ sandigdhe 'hampratyayasyālambanaviśeṣanirṇayāyāha bhagavān ācāryaḥ --
body.translated_text: Therein: the <s>Cārvākas</s> hold that the four elements transformed into the form of the body are the meaning of 'tvam.' Others hold it is each sense organ individually. Others, that it is [the sense organs] combined. Some say it is the mind. Others, <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath). The <s>Saugatāḥ</s> (Buddhists) say it is momentary consciousness. The <s>Mādhyamikas</s> say it is the void (<s>śūnya</s>). The <s>Digambaras</s> (Jains) say it is an entity of body-size, distinct from body and senses. The <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s>, <s>Tārkikas</s> (Naiyāyikas), and <s>Prābhākaras</s> say it is an agent and experiencer that is inert and all-pervading. The <s>Bhāṭṭas</s> say it is inert but of the nature of consciousness. The <s>Sāṅkhyas</s> and <s>Pātañjalas</s> say it is the experiencer alone, of the nature of pure consciousness. The <s>Aupaniṣadas</s> (Vedāntins) say: through <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) it has agency etc., but ultimately it is without attributes, of the very nature of supreme bliss and consciousness. Thus, when the conscious self — established in general through the 'I'-cognition — is rendered doubtful by the conflicting views of disputants, the blessed <s>Ācārya</s> (teacher) says the following, in order to determine the specific object of the 'I'-cognition:

children.text: na bhūmir na toyaṃ na tejo na vāyur na khaṃ nendriyaṃ vā na teṣāṃ samūhaḥ /
children.translated_text: I am not earth, not water, not fire, not air, not space, not a sense organ, nor their aggregate.

children.text: anaikāntikatvāt suṣuptyekasiddhas tad eko 'viśiṣṭaś śivaḥ kevalo 'ham // 1 //
children.translated_text: Since these are non-invariable (<s>anaikāntika</s>), that [self] established in deep sleep alone — one, unqualified, auspicious (<s>Śiva</s>), absolute — that am I. // 1 //

body.text: aham ahampratyayālambanam / ekaḥ advitīyaḥ / aviśiṣṭaḥ sarvadvaitabādhe 'py avādhitaḥ / śivaḥ paramānandabodharūpas tasyaiva maṅgalarūpatvāt / kevalo nirdharmakaḥ / tenādvitīyaḥ sarvapramāṇābādhyaḥ paramānandabodha evāhampratyayāvalambanam ity aupaniṣadapakṣa eva śreyān ity arthaḥ / etadupapādanāyetaravādimatāni nirākariṣyan prathamaṃ dehātmavādaṃ nirākaroti na bhūmir na toyaṃ na vāyur na kham iti / tatrāham iti sarvatra pratyekaṃ nañā sambadhyate / yā bhūmiḥ sāhaṃ na bhavāmi yo 'haṃ sa bhūmir na bhavatīti ca parasparatādātmyābhāvo dṛṣṭavyaḥ /
body.translated_text: 'I' (<s>aham</s>) means the object of the 'I'-cognition. 'One' (<s>eka</s>) means non-dual. 'Unqualified' (<s>aviśiṣṭa</s>) means not sublated even when all duality is sublated. 'Auspicious' (<s>Śiva</s>) means of the nature of supreme bliss and consciousness, since that alone has an auspicious nature. 'Absolute' (<s>kevala</s>) means without attributes. Therefore the meaning is: the non-dual, unsublatable by any means of valid knowledge, supreme bliss and consciousness alone is the object of the 'I'-cognition — thus the <s>Aupaniṣada</s> (Vedāntic) position alone is the best. To establish this, [the author], intending to refute the views of the other disputants, first refutes the body-self doctrine with 'not earth, not water, not air, not space.' Therein, the negation 'not' (<s>na</s>) is connected individually with each [element] everywhere: 'that which is earth, I am not that; and that which I am, that is not earth' — thus the mutual non-identity should be understood.

body.text: yady api vādinā pratyekaṃ bhūmyāder ātmatvaṃ nābhyupeyate saṃghātasyaiva tadabhyupagamāt tathāpi tanmate avayavyanaṅgīkārāt pañcamatattvābhyupagamaprasaṅgena ca saṃyogādisambandhānabhyupagamāt saṃhantur abhāvāc ca saṃghāto nopapadyata ity abhipretya pratyekaṃ bhūtanirākaraṇena bhautikadehātmavādo nirākṛtaḥ /
body.translated_text: Although the disputant does not maintain that earth etc. individually are the self — since only the aggregate is maintained as such — nevertheless, in his view, since the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) is not accepted, since there would be the unwanted consequence of accepting a fifth category, since the relation of conjunction etc. is not accepted, and since an aggregator is absent, the aggregate cannot be established. Having intended this, through the individual refutation of each element, the body-self doctrine of the materialists is refuted.

body.text: yady api ca bhūtacatuṣṭayatattvavādino mate āvaraṇābhāvatvenābhimatasya sthirasyāsata ākāśasya dehānupādānatvaṃ tathāpi siddhānte tasya bhāvatvaṃ dehopādānatvādyaṅgīkārāt tatrāpy ātmatvaprasaktyā tannirākṛtam / atha vā na vāyur ityantam eva dehātmavādasya nirākaraṇaṃ na kham iti tu śūnyavādasya khaśabdasya śūnyavācakatvāt /
body.translated_text: And although in the view of the four-element theorist, space — which is accepted as non-existent due to the absence of any covering [quality], and which is permanent — is not a material cause of the body, nevertheless, since in our established doctrine (<s>siddhānta</s>) its reality is accepted along with its being a material cause of the body etc., the refutation of its being the self was also included due to the possibility of its being attributed selfhood. Alternatively, only up to 'not air' is the refutation of the body-self doctrine; 'not space' is the refutation of the void doctrine (<s>śūnyavāda</s>), since the word 'kha' (space) denotes the void.

body.text: nendriyam iti pratyekam indriyāṇām ātmatvanirāsaḥ / na teṣāṃ samūha iti militānāṃ bhūtānāṃ dehāvayavyākāreṇa pariṇatānām indriyāṇāṃ ca militānāṃ nirāsaḥ / pūrvaṃ saṃghātam anabhyupagamya pratyekaṃ bhūtāni nirākṛtāni / adhunā tu saṃghātam abhyupagamyāpi nirākṛtānīti bhedaḥ / bhūtanirākaraṇena bhautikayoḥ prāṇamanasor nirāsaḥ / manonirākaraṇena manovṛtteḥ kṣaṇikavijñānasya dehātiriktasya kartṛtvabhoktṛtvādiviśiṣṭasya ca nirāsaḥ / siddhānte jñānecchāsukhādīnām antaḥkaraṇāśrayatvābhyupagamāt kāmasaṅkalpādīn prakṛtya mana eveti śruteḥ (BAU I.5.3) / tena deham ārabhya kevalabhoktṛparyantānāṃ tattadvādyabhimatānām anātmatvaṃ pratijñātaṃ bhavati tatra hetum āha -- anaikāntikatvād iti / vyabhicāritvāt vināśitvād iti yāvat / ātmano deśakālāparicchinnatvāt pariccchinnānāṃ ghaṭādivad anātmatvāt khabhinnasya cātmatvābhāvāt, ātmana ekatve 'pi sukhaduḥkhādyāśrayāṇām antaḥkaraṇānāṃ bhedābhyupagamād vyavasthopapatteḥ svenaiva svābhāvagrahaṇe virodhāt, grāhyakāle grāhakāsattvāt grāhakasattve grāhyābhāvāt kṛtahānyakṛtābhyāgamaprasaṅgāc ca na tasya dhvaṃsaprāgabhāvau / sadrūpasyātmanaḥ sarvatrānugamāc ca nātyantābhāvasaṃbhavaḥ / dvaitasya mithyātvenādhiṣṭhānasattād ātmyāpannatayaiva siddhatvāt, śuktirajatādivad adhyastatvena tattādātmyabhāvānupapattiḥ / tenātmanā bhāvapratiyogī / abhāvapratiyoginaś ca dehendriyādayaḥ / tenāmī nātmanaḥ / kiṃ tu svaprakāśabodharūpa ātmani advaite 'py anādyanirvacanīyāvidyākalpitā anirvacanīyā eveti siddhāntarahasyam /
body.translated_text: 'Not a sense-organ' — thus, each sense-organ individually is negated as the self. 'Not their aggregate' — this negates the combined elements that have transformed into the form of the body (the composite whole) together with the combined sense-organs. Previously, without accepting the aggregate, the elements were individually negated. But now they are negated even accepting the aggregate — this is the difference. By the negation of the elements, the two elemental products — <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath) and <s>manas</s> (mind) — are negated. By the negation of mind, the mental modification (<s>manovṛtti</s>), momentary consciousness (<s>kṣaṇikavijñāna</s>), [the self] distinct from the body, and [that] qualified by agency and enjoyership are negated. In our [Advaita] doctrine, since knowledge, desire, pleasure, etc. are accepted as having the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) as their locus, [and] from the <s>śruti</s> (scripture): 'desire, volition, etc. — all this is mind' (BĀU I.5.3). Thus, from the body up to the mere enjoyer, the non-selfhood of the positions held by the respective proponents is declared. He states the reason for this — 'because of being non-invariable (<s>anaikāntika</s>),' meaning because of being deviant, i.e., destructible. Since the <s>ātman</s> (self) is unlimited by space and time, limited things are non-self like a pot, etc. And what is different from space (<s>kha</s>) also lacks selfhood. Even though the <s>ātman</s> is one, since the inner organs which are the substrata of pleasure, pain, etc. are accepted as different, orderly arrangement is possible. Because there is a contradiction in grasping one's own nature by oneself; because the grasper does not exist at the time of grasping; and because if the grasper existed, the graspable would be absent — there would be the undesirable consequences of the loss of what has been done and the accrual of what has not been done — therefore it has neither destruction (<s>dhvaṃsa</s>) nor prior non-existence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>). And since the <s>ātman</s>, being of the nature of existence, pervades everything, absolute non-existence is also impossible. Since duality, being false, is established precisely as having the nature of the substratum's existence — like shell-silver, etc., being superimposed — the identity with that [substratum] does not hold. Therefore the <s>ātman</s> is the counter-positive of [positive] existence; and the body, sense-organs, etc. are the counter-positives of non-existence. Therefore these are not the self. Rather, though the <s>ātman</s> is non-dual, of the nature of self-luminous consciousness, these [phenomena] imagined by beginningless and indescribable <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) are themselves indescribable — this is the secret of the doctrine.

body.text: nanu bodharūpa ātmeti tavābhyupagamāt suṣuptau ca bodhābhāvāt gāḍhaṃ mūḍho 'ham āsaṃ na kiñcid avediṣam iti suptotthitasya parāmarśāt katham avyabhicāritā tasyety āśaṅkyāha -- suṣuptyekasiddha iti / ayam arthaḥ / ātmanaḥ suṣuptisākṣitvān na tatra tadabhāvaḥ, anyathā mūḍho 'ham āsam iti parāmarśānupapatteḥ mātṛmānam iti meeyānāṃ vyabhicāritve 'pi tadbhāvābhāvasākṣiṇaḥ kālatraye 'vyabhicārāt /
body.translated_text: Objection: Since you accept that the <s>ātman</s> is of the nature of consciousness (<s>bodha</s>), and since there is an absence of consciousness in deep sleep (<s>suṣupti</s>), as the person who has awakened reflects, 'I was deeply deluded, I did not know anything' — how can there be non-deviation [of consciousness]? Anticipating this, he says: 'Established solely in deep sleep.' The meaning is this: Since the <s>ātman</s> is the witness of deep sleep, there is no absence of consciousness there; otherwise the reflection 'I was deluded' would be impossible. Even if there is deviation in the things being measured — the measurer, the measure, etc. — the witness of the presence and absence of those [states] is non-deviant across all three times.

body.text: nanu pramāśrayaḥ pramātā sa eva kartā bhoktā pradīpavat svaparasādhāraṇasarvabhāsakaś ceti na ghaṭādivat sākṣisāpekṣa iti cet, na, vikāritvena svavikārasākṣitvānupapatteḥ dṛśyasya draṣṭṛtvānupapatteḥ pramātuś ca pariṇāmitvena dṛśyatvāt, ekasya kūṭasthasyaiva sarvasākṣitvāt /
body.translated_text: Objection: The <s>pramātṛ</s> (knower), who is the locus of valid knowledge (<s>pramā</s>), is himself the agent and enjoyer; and like a lamp, he illuminates both himself and others without requiring a witness like a pot, etc. Answer: No, because being subject to modification, it is impossible for it to be a witness of its own modifications; because what is an object of perception (<s>dṛśya</s>) cannot be the seer (<s>draṣṭṛ</s>); and because the <s>pramātṛ</s>, being subject to transformation, is itself an object of perception. Only one who is immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>) can be the witness of all.

body.text: nanu ekaḥ kūṭastho nirdharmakaḥ sākṣī nādriyate 'prāmāṇikatvād iti cet, na, "tam eva bhāntam anubhāti sarva tasya bhāsā sarvam idaṃ vibhāti (SU VI.14, MuU II.2.10, KauU II.5.15), "na dṛṣṭer draṣṭāraṃ paśyeḥ (BAU III.4.2)" "adṛṣṭo draṣṭā, nānyo 'to 'sti draṣṭā (BAU III.7.23)" ityādi vadatā vedāntapramāṇarājena tasyaiva sarvasākṣitvenābhiṣiktatvāt /
body.translated_text: Objection: One immutable, attributeless witness is not accepted, since it lacks validity as a means of knowledge. Answer: No, because the king of <s>Vedānta</s> authorities — [scriptures] which declare 'Him alone shining, everything shines after; by His light all this is illuminated' (ŚU VI.14, MuU II.2.10), 'You cannot see the seer of sight' (BĀU III.4.2), 'The unseen seer; there is no other seer than He' (BĀU III.7.23), etc. — has anointed that very [immutable self] as the witness of all.

body.text: nanu mahad etad indrajālaṃ pramāśrayān kūṭasthān vihāya kūṭasthapramāśrayam eva pramāṇarājaḥ sarvasākṣiṇaṃ karotīti / bāḍham, indrajālam evaitatsvapnavad avidyāvilasitatvāt tathāpi dṣśyasya ghaṭādivaj jaḍatvena kathaṃ pramāśrayatvam iti cet, na, darpaṇādivad atisvacchatvena cidbimbagrāhakatvāc cittād ātmyādhyāsād vā /
body.translated_text: Objection: This is a great illusion — that the king of authorities, abandoning the immutable as the locus of valid knowledge, makes the very immutable locus of knowledge the witness of all! Indeed, this is an illusion, like a dream, since it is the play of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance). Even so, how can what is visible (<s>dṛśya</s>), being inert like a pot, be the locus of valid knowledge? Answer: No, because like a mirror, being extremely transparent, it can receive the reflection of consciousness (<s>cidbimba</s>); or because of the superimposition of selfhood from consciousness (<s>citta</s>).

body.text: nanu nīrūpasya niravayavasyāatmanaḥ kathaṃ pratibimba iti cet, kātrānupapattiḥ, vibhramahetūnāṃ vicitratvāt, japākusumarūpasya nīrūpasya niravayavasyāpi sphaṭikādau pratibimbadarśanāc chabdasyāpi pratiśabdākhyapratibimbopalambhāt tayoḥ sampratipannapratibimbavailakṣaṇyanirūpaṇāt /
body.translated_text: Objection: How can there be a reflection of the <s>ātman</s>, which is formless and partless? Answer: Where is the impossibility here? Because the causes of illusion are diverse; and because we observe the reflection of the <s>japā</s> (hibiscus) flower — which is formless and partless — in a crystal, etc.; and because even of sound, a reflection called echo (<s>pratiśabda</s>) is perceived; and because the dissimilarity of those well-known reflections can be demonstrated.

body.text: tathāpīndriyagrāhyasyaiva pratibimba iti cet, na, vyabhicārāt, anindriyagrāhyasākṣipratyakṣasyāpy ākāśasyāpi jalādau pratibimbopalambhāt / anyathā jānumātre 'py udake atigambhīra(tā)pratītir na syāt / tarhi andhasya jale pratibimbapratītiḥ kuto na jāyate sālokasya sābhrasya pratibimbitatvāt tadgrahaṇārthaṃ cakṣuṣo 'pekṣaṇāt / etena nīlaṃ nabha ityādivibhrame 'pi cakṣuranvayavyatirekau vyākhyātau tatra sālokasyākāśasyādhiṣṭhānatvāt / tasmāc cākṣuṣapratibimbam eva rūpasāpekṣam ity avadheyam /
body.translated_text: Objection: But reflection belongs only to what is graspable by the senses. Answer: No, because of deviation — since even of space (<s>ākāśa</s>), which is not graspable by the senses [but is] perceived by the witness-perception (<s>sākṣipratyakṣa</s>), a reflection is observed in water, etc. Otherwise, the perception of extreme depth even in knee-deep water would not occur. Then why does a blind person not have a perception of reflection in water? Because the sky, along with its light, along with its clouds, is reflected, and the eye is required for grasping that [reflection]. By this, the presence and absence of the eye in illusions such as 'the sky is blue' is also explained; there the sky along with its light serves as the substratum. Therefore, it should be noted that visual reflection alone requires form [as a condition].

body.text: tathāpy ātmanaḥ pratibimbe kiṃ pramāṇam iti cet, śṛṇu -- "rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva tad asya rūpaṃ praticakṣaṇāya (BAU II.5.19)" "māyābhāsena jīveśau karoti (NU 9)" "ekadhā bahudhā caiva dṣśyate jalacandravat (BBU 12)" ityādiśrutiḥ, "sa eṣa iha praviṣṭaḥ (BAU I.4.7)" "sa etam eva sīmānaṃ vidāryaitayādvārā prāpadyata (AitU I.3.12)" "tatsṛṣṭvā tad evānuprāviśat (TU II.6.1)" ityādi praveśaśrutyanyathānupapattiḥ "ābhāsa eva ca (BS II.3.50)" "ata eva copamāssuryakādivat (BS III.2.18)" ityādipāramarṣasūtraṇi ca tatra mānāni /
body.translated_text: Even so, what is the authority for the reflection of the <s>ātman</s>? Listen — <s>Śruti</s> (scripture) texts such as: 'He became the counter-form of every form; that is His form, for the purpose of making Him seen' (BĀU II.5.19); 'By the semblance of <s>māyā</s>, He creates the <s>jīva</s> and <s>Īśvara</s>' (NU 9); 'Though one, He is seen as many, like the moon in water' (BBU 12). Also, <s>śrutis</s> on 'entering' — 'He entered right here' (BĀU I.4.7); 'Having split open this very seam, He entered through that door' (AitU I.3.12); 'Having created it, He entered into that very [creation]' (TU II.6.1) — which are otherwise inexplicable. And <s>Brahmasūtras</s> such as: 'It is merely a semblance (<s>ābhāsa</s>)' (BS II.3.50); 'Therefore, by analogy, like the sun, etc.' (BS III.2.18) — these are the authorities in this matter.

body.text: tasya ca pratibimbasya satyam eveti pratibimbavādinaḥ, mithyātvam evety ābhāsavādinaḥ / svarūpe tu na vivāda evety anyad etat / acetanavilakṣaṇatvaṃ tu tasya śrutisiddham anubhavasiddhaṃ ca / tasmāt siddham antaḥkaraṇasya pratibimbādhyāsadvārā pramātṛtvam /
body.translated_text: Regarding that reflection: the <s>Pratibimbavādins</s> (reflection theorists) [hold] it is real; the <s>Ābhāsavādins</s> (semblance theorists) [hold] it is false. But regarding the essential nature [of <s>Brahman</s>], there is no dispute at all — this is a different matter. That [reflection's] difference from the insentient is established both by <s>śruti</s> and by experience. Therefore it is established that the <s>antaḥkaraṇa</s> (inner organ) has the status of knower (<s>pramātṛtva</s>) through the medium of reflection or superimposition.

body.text: nanu, adhyāso 'pi nopapadyate / tathāhi -- ātmani vā anātmādhyasyate anātmany ātmā vā / nādyaḥ, tasya niḥsāmānyaviśeṣavatvena sarvadābhāsamānatvena sādṛśyādirahitatvena cādhiṣṭhānatvāsambhavāt / nāpi dvitīyaḥ, tasya mithyātvābhyupagamāt / mithyāvastuno 'dhiṣṭhānatve śūnyavādaprasaṅgāt / tasya ca satyatve tadanivṛtter anirmokṣaprasaṅgāc ca / na hi satyaṃ kvacin nivartate, nivartamānaṃ vā bhramajñānena / śrutayaś ca "bhidyate hṛdayagranthiś chidyante sarvasaṃśayāḥ / kṣīyante cāsya karmāṇi tasmin dṛṣṭe parāvare (MU II.2.8)" "tam eva viditvātimṛtyum eti nānyaḥ panthā vidyate ayanāya (SU III.8)" "tarati śokam ātmavit (ChU VII.1.3)" ityādyāḥ jñānāt sarvasaṃsāranivṛttiṃ darśayantyaḥ tasya mithyātvaṃ sūcayanti / "ekam evādvitīyam (ChU VI.2.1)" "ato 'nyad ārtam (BAU III.4.2)" "neha nānāsti kiṃcana (BAU IV.4.19)" "athāta ādeśo neti neti (BAU II.3.6)" ityādyāḥ śrutayaḥ sākṣād eva mithyātvaṃ pratipādayanti / dṛśyatvena śuktirajatavan mithyātvānumānac ca / ātmanya adhyastatayaiva cānātmani siddhe tatrātmādhyāsaḥ / anātmādhyāsena cātmano doṣasādṛśyādisambhavāt tatra cānātmādhyāsa ityātmāśrayādidoṣaprasaṅgāc ca / etenātmānātmādhyāsasyāvidyākalpitatvān na vikalpāvasara ity apāstam svaprakāśātmany avidyāyā apy anupapatteḥ / tathāhi sāpi adhyastānadhyastā vā / tatrādye kathaṃ nātmāśrayādidoṣaprasaṅgaḥ / antye tasyā anucchedād anirmokṣaprasaṅaḥ / sarvasyādhyāsamūlatve ca bhramapramādivyavasthā na syāt / ekasyaivātmanaḥ pramāṇaprameyapramitipramātṛrūpatā ca viruddhā, avirodhābhyupagame vā saugatam atopapattir iti /
body.translated_text: Objection: Superimposition (<s>adhyāsa</s>) too is impossible. For: either the non-self is superimposed on the <s>ātman</s>, or the <s>ātman</s> on the non-self. Not the first, because the <s>ātman</s>, having neither universal nor particular [attributes], being always self-manifest, and being devoid of similarity, etc., cannot serve as a substratum [for superimposition]. Nor the second, because the non-self is accepted as false; and if something false were the substratum, the <s>Śūnyavāda</s> (doctrine of voidness) would follow. And if the non-self were real, there would be no cessation of it and hence no liberation. For what is real never ceases anywhere, nor [does it cease] through knowledge of illusion. And <s>śrutis</s> such as 'The knot of the heart is pierced, all doubts are cut asunder, and one's karmas are destroyed, when That — the higher and the lower — is seen' (MU II.2.8); 'Knowing Him alone, one crosses beyond death; there is no other path for going' (ŚU III.8); 'The knower of the self crosses over sorrow' (ChU VII.1.3) — showing the cessation of all <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly bondage) through knowledge — indicate its falsity. <s>Śrutis</s> such as 'One only, without a second' (ChU VI.2.1); 'Anything other than this is afflicted' (BĀU III.4.2); 'There is no diversity here whatsoever' (BĀU IV.4.19); 'Now the teaching: not this, not this' (BĀU II.3.6) — directly teach its falsity. And there is also the inference of falsity from being an object of perception, like shell-silver. And since the non-self is established precisely as superimposed on the <s>ātman</s>, the superimposition of the <s>ātman</s> on it [follows]. And since through the superimposition of the non-self, qualities like defect and similarity become possible for the <s>ātman</s>, the superimposition of the non-self upon it [also follows] — and so faults like mutual dependence (<s>ātmāśraya</s>) would arise. [Opponent:] By this [argument], since the mutual superimposition of self and non-self is imagined by <s>avidyā</s>, there is no occasion for such alternatives — this is set aside, because <s>avidyā</s> itself is impossible with respect to the self-luminous <s>ātman</s>. For [<s>avidyā</s>] too is either superimposed or not superimposed. In the first case, how would the fault of mutual dependence not arise? In the latter case, since it would not be sublated, there would be no liberation. And if everything were rooted in superimposition, the orderly distinction between error and valid knowledge would not hold. And for the one <s>ātman</s> to have the forms of means of knowledge, object of knowledge, resultant knowledge, and knower would be contradictory; or if non-contradiction were accepted, the Buddhist position, not [ours], would be established.

body.text: atrocyate -- ahaṃ manuṣyah kartā bhoktetyādipratītis tāvat sarvajanasiddhā / sā ca na smṛtir aparokṣāvabhāsatvād bhedāgrahapūrvakatvāc ca /
body.translated_text: Here it is said: The cognition "I am a human being, I am an agent, I am an experiencer" and so forth is established for all people. And this is not memory (<s>smṛti</s>), since it has the nature of immediate (non-mediate) appearance, and since it is not preceded by the apprehension of difference.

body.text: nāpi pramā śrutiyuktibādhitatvāt / tathā ca śrutayaḥ "yo 'yaṃ vijñānamayaḥ prāṇeṣu hṛdyantarjyotiḥ puruṣaḥ (BAU IV.3.7)" "ayam ātmā brahma (BAU II.5.19)" "satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma (TU II.1)" "vijñānam ānandaṃ brahma (BAU III.9.28)" "ya ātmā apahatapāpmā (ChU VI.7.1)" yat sākṣād aparokṣād brahma ya ātmā sarvāntaraḥ (BAU III.4.1)" "yo 'śanāyāpipāse śokaṃ mohaṃ jarāṃ mṛtyum atyeti (BAU III.5.1)" "sa yat tatra kiñcit paśyati ananvāgatas tena bhavati asaṅgo hy ayaṃ puruṣaḥ (BAU IV.3.15)" ityādyā akartṛbhoktṛparamānandarūpatām ātmano darśayanti / yuktaś ca
body.translated_text: Nor is it valid knowledge (<s>pramā</s>), because it is contradicted by <s>śruti</s> (scripture) and reasoning. The <s>śrutis</s> are as follows: "This person who consists of intelligence, the inner light among the vital breaths, within the heart" (BAU IV.3.7), "This self is <s>Brahman</s>" (BAU II.5.19), "<s>Brahman</s> is truth, knowledge, infinite" (TU II.1), "<s>Brahman</s> is intelligence and bliss" (BAU III.9.28), "The self that is free from evil" (ChU VI.7.1), "That which is directly and immediately <s>Brahman</s>, the self that is innermost of all" (BAU III.4.1), "He who transcends hunger, thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age, and death" (BAU III.5.1), "Whatever he sees there, he is not followed by it, for this <s>puruṣa</s> (person) is unattached" (BAU IV.3.15) — these and other texts show the self's nature as non-agent, non-experiencer, and of the form of supreme bliss. And by reasoning:

body.text: vikārī paricchinnatvenānātmatvāpatteḥ svenaiva svasya grahaṇe kartṛkarmavirodhāt dṛgdṛśyayoś ca sambandhānupapatteḥ bhedenābhedena vā dharmadharmibhāvānupapatteś ca / jñānānityatvapakṣe tattadvyaktibhedadhvaṃsaprāgabhāvasamavāyajñānatvajātyādyabhyupagame gauravāt, ekatvābhyupagame cātilāghavāt, ghaṭajñānaṃ paṭajñānam ity upādhibhedapuraskāreṇaiva jñānabhedapratīteḥ / svatas tu jñānaṃ jñānam iti ekasvarūpāvagamāt, tadutpattivināśapratītyoś cāvaśyakalpyaviṣayasambandhaviṣayatayāpy upapatteḥ, upādhiparāmarśam antareṇa svata eva ghaṭād ghaṭāntarasya bhedapratītes tatpratibandīgrahāsambhavād ākāśakāladiśām api nānātvāpatteś ca /
body.translated_text: Because what is subject to modification (<s>vikārin</s>), being limited, would entail the consequence of being non-self; because in self-apprehension by oneself there would be a contradiction between agent and object; because the relation between seer and seen cannot be established; and because the relation of property and property-bearer cannot be established either through difference or through non-difference. If knowledge is held to be non-eternal, then by accepting the destruction, prior non-existence, inherence, knowledge-ness, universal, and the like as distinct for each particular instance, there is the fault of excessive complexity (<s>gaurava</s>). And if unity is accepted, there is excessive simplicity (<s>atilāghava</s>). [Moreover,] the cognition of difference in knowledge — 'pot-knowledge,' 'cloth-knowledge' — is based solely on the difference of limiting adjuncts (<s>upādhi</s>). But intrinsically, knowledge as knowledge is apprehended as one in nature. And the cognitions of its origination and destruction can also be explained as having for their object a necessarily posited connection with objects. And because, without reference to limiting adjuncts, the cognition of difference between one pot and another pot intrinsically is impossible — since the counter-correlate apprehension [needed for such difference] is impossible — the consequence would be multiplicity even of space, time, and direction.

body.text: kartṛtvāder vāstavatve 'nirmokṣaprasaṅgāt /
body.translated_text: And if agency and the like were real, there would be the unwelcome consequence of the impossibility of liberation.

body.text: svaprakāśānabhyupagame ca jagadāndhyaprasaṅgāt, paramapremāspadatvena ca tasyānandarūpatvāt, nirdharmakanityasvaprakāśasukhātmaka evātmā ityādayaḥ /
body.translated_text: And if self-luminosity is not accepted, there would be the unwelcome consequence of universal blindness. And since the self is the object of supreme love, it must be of the nature of bliss. Therefore, the self is only of the nature of attributeless, eternal, self-luminous happiness — such are the [arguments from reasoning].

body.text: tasmāt pariśeṣād bhrāntir iyam iti sthite tatkāraṇam api yogyaṃ kiñcit kalpanīyam / kalpyamānaṃ ca tadātmany adhyastatayaiva dharmigrāhakamānena sidhyatīti na jānāmīti sākṣipratītisiddham anirvācyam ajñānam eva tat / na cedam abhāvarūpam, jñānasya nityatvena tadabhāvānupapatter uktatvāt /
body.translated_text: Therefore, it being established by the method of elimination that this [cognition] is error (<s>bhrānti</s>), some fitting cause for it must also be postulated. And what is postulated is established only as superimposed upon the self, through the means of knowledge that apprehends the substrate (<s>dharmin</s>). Hence 'I do not know' — the indeterminable <s>ajñāna</s> (ignorance), established through the witness-cognition (<s>sākṣipratīti</s>), is that [cause]. And this is not of the nature of mere absence (<s>abhāva</s>), because it has been stated that, knowledge being eternal, the absence of knowledge cannot be established.

body.text: dharmipratiyogijñānājñānābhyāṃ ca vyāghātāpatteḥ / nāpi bhramasaṃśayatatsaṃskāraparamparārupam, aparokṣatvāt, atītānāgatabhramasaṃśayatatsaṃskārāṇāṃ cāparokṣatvena jñātum aśakyatvāt, āvaraṇātmakatvāt, bhramādyutpādanatvāc ca / ātmano nirvikāratvāt, antaḥkaraṇādeś ca tajjanyatvāt, "devātmaśaktiṃ svaguṇair nigūḍhām (SU I.3)" iti guṇavattvaśruteś ca "māyāṃ tu prakṛtiṃ vidyān māyinaṃ tu maheśvaram (SU IV.10)"
body.translated_text: And because there would be the unwelcome consequence of contradiction between knowledge and ignorance as counter-correlates of the same substrate. Nor is it of the nature of error, doubt, or the chain of impressions thereof, because [<s>ajñāna</s>] is immediate (<s>aparokṣa</s>), because past and future errors, doubts, and their impressions cannot be known as immediate, because [<s>ajñāna</s>] has the nature of concealment (<s>āvaraṇa</s>), and because it produces error and the like. Because the self is changeless, and because the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) and the like are its products. And because of the <s>śruti</s> declaring it to possess qualities: "The power belonging to the divine self, concealed by its own qualities" (ŚU I.3). And "Know <s>māyā</s> to be <s>prakṛti</s> (nature), and the possessor of <s>māyā</s> to be the great Lord" (ŚU IV.10).

body.text: "indro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate (BAU II.5.19)" "anṛtena hi pratyūḍhāḥ (ChU VIII.3.2)" "nīhāreṇa prāvṛttāḥ (TS IV.6.2.2)" "bhūyaś cānte viśvamāyānivṛttiḥ (SU I.10)" ityādiśruteś ca māyāvidyānirvācyam anṛtaṃ tattvajñānanivartyañ cājñānam eva svaparādhyāse kāraṇam /
body.translated_text: "<s>Indra</s> moves in many forms through <s>māyā</s>" (BAU II.5.19), "For they are covered over by the untrue" (ChU VIII.3.2), "Covered by mist" (TS IV.6.2.2), "And at the end, the cessation of universal <s>māyā</s>" (ŚU I.10) — from these and other <s>śruti</s> passages, <s>māyā</s>, <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), the indeterminable, the untrue, that which is removable by the knowledge of reality — this <s>ajñāna</s> alone is the cause of the superimposition upon oneself and upon others.

body.text: na cātmāśrayādidoṣaprasaṅgaḥ, anāditvena tannirāsāt, anāditvenotpattyabhāvāt, svaprakāśātmana eva tajjñaptirūpatvāt /
body.translated_text: And there is no fault of self-dependence (<s>ātmāśraya</s>) and the like, since this is negated by [<s>ajñāna</s>'s] beginninglessness. Because being beginningless, there is no origination [requiring a cause]. And because the cognition of it is of the nature of the self-luminous self itself.

body.text: tenājñānādhyāsaḥ, tadviśiṣṭe caitanye 'haṅkārādhyāsaḥ, tadviśiṣṭe ca kāmasaṅkalpādīnām ahaṅkāradharmāṇām indriyadharmāṇāṃ ca kāṇatvabadhiratvādīnām adhyāḥ /
body.translated_text: From that, there is the superimposition of <s>ajñāna</s> (ignorance) [upon the self]; upon consciousness qualified by that, there is the superimposition of the ego-sense (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>); and upon [consciousness] qualified by that, there is the superimposition of desire, volition, and the like — which are properties of the ego-sense — as well as the properties of the sense-organs such as blindness, deafness, and the like.

body.text: indriyāṇāṃ tu parokṣatvān nāparokṣadharmyadhyāsa iti siddhāntaḥ /
body.translated_text: But since the sense-organs are indirect (<s>parokṣa</s>), there is no superimposition of them as immediate (<s>aparokṣa</s>) substrates — this is the established doctrine.

body.text: tadviśiṣṭe ca sthūladehādhyāsaḥ, dharmipuraskāreṇaivāhaṃ manuṣya ity ākāraḥ, na tu svarūpato 'haṃ deha ity adhyāsaḥ, tathā pratītyabhāvāt / tadviśiṣṭe ca sthaulyādīnāṃ dehadharmāṇām adhyāsaḥ /
body.translated_text: And upon [consciousness] qualified by that, there is the superimposition of the gross body, taking the form 'I am a human being,' with the substrate as the primary element — but there is no superimposition of the form 'I am the body' in its essential nature, because such a cognition does not occur. And upon [consciousness] qualified by that, there is the superimposition of the properties of the body, such as corpulence and the like.

body.text: tadviśiṣṭe bāhyānāṃ putrabhāryādīnāṃ sākalyavaikalyādidharmādhyāsaḥ / evaṃ caitanyasyāpy ahaṅkārādiṣu dehaparyanteṣv adhyāsaḥ saṃsargataḥ / adhyāsavyavadhānatāratamyāc ca prematāratamyam / tad uktaṃ vārtikāmṛe (BAUBhV I.4.1031) --
body.translated_text: And upon [consciousness] qualified by that, there is the superimposition of external things such as son, wife, and the like, along with properties such as completeness and incompleteness. Thus, consciousness too is superimposed upon the ego-sense and so forth, down to the body, through association. And the gradation in love corresponds to the gradation in the degree of superimposition. As stated in the <s>Vārtikāmṛta</s> (BAUBhV I.4.1031):

children.text: vittāt putraḥ priyaḥ putrāt piṇḍaḥ piṇḍāt tathendriyam /
children.translated_text: "Dearer than wealth is the son; dearer than the son is the body (<s>piṇḍa</s>); dearer than the body are the senses;

children.text: indriyebhyaḥ priyaḥ prāṇaḥ prāṇād ātmā paraḥ priyaḥ // iti //
children.translated_text: dearer than the senses is the vital breath (<s>prāṇa</s>); and dearer than the vital breath is the self (<s>ātman</s>)."

body.text: piṇḍaḥ sthūlaśarīram, prāṇo'ntaḥkaraṇam / dehāpekṣayā cendriyāṇāṃ priyatvaṃ śastravṛṣṭyādidhārāpāte cakṣuṣo nimīlanadarśanād anubhavasiddham / tenānyonyādhyāsāc cidacidgranthirūpo 'dhyāsaḥ /
body.translated_text: The 'body' (<s>piṇḍa</s>) means the gross body; '<s>prāṇa</s>' means the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>). And the greater dearness of the senses compared to the body is established by experience, from the observed closing of the eyes when a rain of weapons falls — [one protects the senses even at the cost of the body]. Therefore, from this mutual superimposition, the superimposition has the nature of a knot (<s>granthi</s>) between consciousness and insentience.

body.text: ekatarasyādhyāsāṅgīkāre 'nyatarasyābhānaprasaṅgāt, adhyastasyaiva bhrame bhānaniyamāt (SS I.36) "ime raṅgarajate" iti samūhālambanabhramavad avaśyam itaretarādhyāsaḥ / sarvabādhāvadhibhūtacaitanyapariśeṣeṇa ca na śūnyavādāpattiḥ, satyānṛtasaṃbhedāvabhāsatvād adhyāsasya / tasmāt pūrvapūrvādhyāsamūla evāyam uttarottaro 'haṅkārādyadhyāso bījāṅkuravad anādiḥ / avidyādhyāsaś ca eka evānādiḥ /
body.translated_text: Because if the superimposition of only one [upon the other] is accepted, there would be the unwelcome consequence of the non-appearance of the other — since in error, it is a rule that only what is superimposed appears (SS I.36). Like the collective erroneous cognition 'these are colored as silver' [where both shell and silver appear], mutual superimposition between the two is necessary. And through the residual method — pure consciousness being that which remains when all [superimpositions] are sublated — there is no fall into the doctrine of the void (<s>śūnyavāda</s>), since superimposition has the nature of the appearance of a blend of the real and the unreal. Therefore, each successive superimposition of the ego-sense and the like is rooted in the preceding superimposition, like the seed and sprout, and is beginningless. And the superimposition of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) is the one and only beginningless [root].

body.text: nanv adhyāsasyānāditve "smṛtirūpaḥ paratra pūrvadṛṣṭāvabhāso 'dhyāsa (BSBh)" iti vadatā bhāṣyakāreṇa smṛtirūpatvena saṃskārajanyatvam uktaṃ viruddhyeta iti cet, na, kāryādhyāsābhiprāyatvāt tasya, paratra parāvabhāsa ity etāvan mātrasyaiva ubhayānugatasya lakṣaṇatvāt /
body.translated_text: Objection: If superimposition is beginningless, it would contradict the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> (<s>Śaṅkara</s>) who says "Superimposition is the apparent presentation, in the form of memory, of something previously perceived, in something else" (BSBh) — since by [defining it as] having the form of memory, he states that it is produced from impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>). Reply: No, because that [definition] refers to the superimposition of effects (<s>kāryādhyāsa</s>). The essential definition, applicable to both [causal and effectual superimposition], is merely this much: 'the apparent presentation of one thing in another.'

body.text: yad vā "satyānṛte mithunīkṛtya (BSBh)" iti bhāṣyakāravacanāt satyamithyāvastusaṃbhedāvabhāso 'dhyāsa ity eva siddhāntalakṣaṇam / tena kāraṇādhyāse 'pi na lakṣaṇāvyāptiḥ / kāryādhyasasya ca pravāharūpeṇa bījāṅkuravad anāditvābhidhānān na ko 'pi doṣaḥ /
body.translated_text: Alternatively, from the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>'s statement "coupling together the real and the unreal" (BSBh), the established definition of superimposition is the appearance of a blend of a real entity and an unreal entity. By this definition, there is no failure of the definition to apply even to causal superimposition (<s>kāraṇādhyāsa</s>). And since the effectual superimposition is described as beginningless in the form of a stream, like seed and sprout, there is no fault whatsoever.

body.text: evam adhyāse siddhe ekasyāpy ātmano jīveśvarādivyavasthā mānameyādipratikarmavyavasthā copapadyate / tathā hi -- ajñānopahita ātmā ajñānatādātmyāpannaḥ svacidābhāsāvivekād antaryāmī sākṣī jagatkāraṇam iti ca kathyate, buddhyupahitaś ca tattādātmyāpannaḥ svacidābhāsāvivekāj jīvaḥ kartā bhoktā pramāteti ca kathyata iti vārtikakārapādāḥ /
body.translated_text: Thus, with superimposition established, the distinction of the one self into <s>jīva</s> (individual soul) and <s>Īśvara</s> (Lord), as well as the systematic arrangement of the means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, and so forth, are explained. Namely: the self conditioned by <s>ajñāna</s> (ignorance), having assumed identity with <s>ajñāna</s>, due to non-discrimination from its own reflected consciousness (<s>cidābhāsa</s>), is called the inner controller (<s>antaryāmī</s>), the witness (<s>sākṣin</s>), and the cause of the universe. And the self conditioned by the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>), having assumed identity with it, due to non-discrimination from its own reflected consciousness, is called the <s>jīva</s> (individual soul), the agent, the experiencer, and the knower — thus [teach] the feet of the <s>Vārtikakāra</s> (<s>Sureśvara</s>).

body.text: pratidehaṃ buddhīnāṃ ca bhinnatvāt tadgatacidābhāsabhedena tadaviviktaṃ caitanyam api bhinnam iva pratīyate / ajñānasya tu sarvatrābhinnatvāt tadgatacidābhāsabhedābhāvāt tadaviviktasākṣicaitanyasya na kadācid api bhedabhānam iti /
body.translated_text: And since the intellects (<s>buddhis</s>) are different for each body, the consciousness that is undiscriminated from the reflected consciousness (<s>cidābhāsa</s>) in each of them appears as if different, due to the difference of the reflected consciousness in each. But since <s>ajñāna</s> (ignorance) is undifferentiated everywhere, there being no difference of reflected consciousness in it, the witness-consciousness (<s>sākṣicaitanya</s>) undiscriminated from it never appears as different.

body.text: asmiṃś ca pakṣe tattvamādipade jahallakṣanaiva sābhāsasyopādher vācyārthāṃśasya hānād ābhāsasyāpi jaḍājaḍavilakṣaṇatvenānirvacanīyatvāt / tad uktaṃ saṅkṣepaśārīrake --
body.translated_text: And on this view, in the [great] sentences such as 'That thou art' (<s>tat tvam asi</s>), the secondary meaning (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) is of the <s>jahal</s> (exclusive) type alone, since the limiting adjunct (<s>upādhi</s>) along with the reflection is the expressed meaning-portion that is abandoned, and since even the reflection, being neither sentient nor insentient, is indeterminable. As stated in the <s>Saṅkṣepaśārīraka</s>:

children.text: sābhāsājñānavācī yadi bhavati punar brahmaśabdas tathāhaṃ /
children.translated_text: "If the word '<s>Brahman</s>' denotes [<s>Brahman</s>] along with the reflection and <s>ajñāna</s>, and likewise if the word 'I'

children.text: śabdo 'haṅkāravācī bhavati tu jahatī lakṣaṇā tatra pakṣe // iti //
children.translated_text: denotes the ego-sense, then the <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification) in that case is the <s>jahatī</s> (exclusive) type."

body.text: na cābhāsasyaiva baddhatvāt kevalacaitanyasya ca muktatvād bandhamokṣayor vaiyadhikaraṇyaṃ svanāśārthaṃ pravṛttyanupapattiś ceti vācyam, kevalacaitanyasyaivābhāsadvārā baddhatvābhyupagamāt, taduktaṃ vārtikakārapādaiḥ --
body.translated_text: Nor should it be objected that since it is the reflection (<s>ābhāsa</s>) alone that is bound, and pure consciousness that is liberated, bondage and liberation would belong to different loci, and that there would be the impossibility of effort aimed at one's own destruction — because it is accepted that pure consciousness itself is bound through the medium of the reflection. As stated by the feet of the <s>Vārtikakāra</s> (<s>Sureśvara</s>):

body.text: "ayam eva hi no 'nartho yat saṃsāry ātmadarśanam (BUBhV)" iti /
body.translated_text: "This alone is our misfortune: the vision of the self as a <s>saṃsārin</s> (transmigrant)." (BUBhV)

body.text: tena śuddhacaitanyasyābhāsa eva bandhaḥ, tannivṛttiś ca mokṣa iti na kiñcidasamañjasam / atha vābhāsāviviktaṃ caitanyam api tattvamādipadavācyam / tena vācyaikadeśasyātyāgād asmin pakṣe jahadajahallakṣaṇaiveti na ko 'pi doṣaḥ / ayam eva pakṣa ābhāsavāda iti gīyate /
body.translated_text: Therefore, for pure consciousness, the reflection (<s>ābhāsa</s>) alone is bondage, and its cessation is liberation — thus there is nothing inconsistent. Alternatively, consciousness undiscriminated from the reflection may also be considered the meaning of the words 'That' and 'thou' and so forth [in the great sentences]. Since on this view a part of the expressed meaning is not abandoned, the <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification) on this view is of the <s>jahadajahal</s> (inclusive-exclusive) type — thus there is no fault whatsoever. This very view is celebrated as the <s>ābhāsavāda</s> (doctrine of reflection).

body.text: ajñānopahitaṃ bimbacaitanyam īśvaraḥ, antaḥkaraṇatatsaṃskārāvacchinnājñānapratibimbitaṃ caitanyaṃ jīva iti vivaraṇakārāḥ / ajñānapratibimbitaṃ caitanyam īśvaraḥ, buddhipratibimbitaṃ caitanyaṃ jīvaḥ, ajñānopahitaṃ tu bimbacaitanyaṃ śuddham iti saṅkṣepaśārīrakakārāḥ / anayoś ca pakṣayoḥ buddhibhedāj jīvanānātvam / pratibimbasya ca pāramārthikatvāj jahallakṣaṇaiva tattvamādipadeṣu / imam eva pratibimbavādam ācakṣate /
body.translated_text: According to the <s>Vivaraṇa</s> school: <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord) is the original (<s>bimba</s>) consciousness conditioned by <s>ajñāna</s> (ignorance); the <s>jīva</s> (individual self) is consciousness reflected in <s>ajñāna</s> as delimited by the <s>antaḥkaraṇa</s> (inner organ) and its impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>). According to the author of the <s>Saṅkṣepaśārīraka</s>: <s>Īśvara</s> is consciousness reflected in <s>ajñāna</s>; the <s>jīva</s> is consciousness reflected in the <s>buddhi</s> (intellect); while the original (<s>bimba</s>) consciousness conditioned by <s>ajñāna</s> is pure. In both these positions, the multiplicity of <s>jīvas</s> is due to the difference in <s>buddhis</s>. And since the reflection is ultimately real, in statements like 'That thou art,' only <s>jahal-lakṣaṇā</s> (exclusive secondary meaning) applies. This is called the <s>pratibimba-vāda</s> (reflection theory).

body.text: ajñānaviṣayībhūtaṃ caitanyam īśvaraḥ, ajñānāśrayībhūtaṃ ca jīva iti vācaspatimiśrāḥ / asmiṃś ca pakṣe ajñānanānātvāj jīvanānātvam /
body.translated_text: According to <s>Vācaspatimiśra</s>: <s>Īśvara</s> is consciousness that is the object of <s>ajñāna</s>; the <s>jīva</s> is consciousness that is the locus of <s>ajñāna</s>. In this position, the multiplicity of <s>jīvas</s> is due to the multiplicity of <s>ajñānas</s>.

body.text: pratijīvaṃ ca prapañcabhedaḥ, jīvasyaiva svājñānopahitatayā jagadupādānatvāt / pratyabhijñā ca atisādṛśyāt / īśvarasya ca saprapañcajīvāvidyādhiṣṭhānatvena kāraṇatvopacārād iti / ayam eva cāvacchedavādaḥ /
body.translated_text: And the differentiation of the phenomenal world is individual to each <s>jīva</s>, since the <s>jīva</s> itself — being conditioned by its own <s>ajñāna</s> — is the material cause (<s>upādāna</s>) of the world. Mutual recognition [among jīvas of the same world] is due to extreme similarity. And <s>Īśvara</s> is called the cause only figuratively, insofar as he is the substratum (<s>adhiṣṭhāna</s>) of the <s>avidyā</s> of the <s>jīvas</s> along with their phenomenal worlds. This is the <s>avaccheda-vāda</s> (limitation theory).

body.text: ajñānopahitaṃ bimbacaitanyam īśvaraḥ, ajñānapratibimbitaṃ caitanyaṃ jīva iti vā, ajñānānupahitaṃ śuddhacaitanyam īśvaraḥ, ajñānopahitaṃ jīva iti vā, mukhyo vedāntasiddhānta ekajīvavādākhyaḥ / imam eva ca dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivādam ācakṣate / asmiṃś ca pakṣe jīva eva svājñānavaśāj jagadupādānaṃ nimittaṃ ca, dṣśyaṃ ca sarvaṃ praītikam / dehabhedāc ca jīvabhedabhrāntiḥ / ekasyaiva ca svakalpitaguruśāstrādyupabṛṃhitaśravaṇamananādidārḍhyād ātmasākṣātkāre sati mokṣaḥ / śukādīnāṃ mokṣaśravaṇaṃ cārthavāda eva / mahāvākye ca tatpadamanantasatyādipadavadajñānānupahitacaitanyasya lakṣaṇayopasthāpakam ityādyā avāntarabhedāḥ svayam ūhanīyāḥ /
body.translated_text: The principal <s>Vedānta</s> doctrine, called <s>ekajīva-vāda</s> (the single-self theory), holds either that: <s>Īśvara</s> is the original consciousness conditioned by <s>ajñāna</s> and the <s>jīva</s> is consciousness reflected in <s>ajñāna</s>; or that: <s>Īśvara</s> is pure consciousness unconditioned by <s>ajñāna</s> and the <s>jīva</s> is consciousness conditioned by <s>ajñāna</s>. This is also called the <s>dṛṣṭi-sṛṣṭi-vāda</s> (the theory that perception is creation). In this position, the <s>jīva</s> itself, by the power of its own <s>ajñāna</s>, is both the material and efficient cause of the world; and everything perceived is merely apparent (<s>prātītika</s>). The appearance of multiple <s>jīvas</s> is an illusion due to bodily differences. <s>Mokṣa</s> (liberation) occurs for this single [jīva] when direct realization of the self (<s>ātma-sākṣātkāra</s>) arises through the firmness of <s>śravaṇa</s> (hearing), <s>manana</s> (reflection), etc., strengthened by self-imagined teachers, scriptures, and the like. The scriptural accounts of the liberation of <s>Śuka</s> and others are merely <s>arthavāda</s> (eulogistic passages). And in the <s>mahāvākya</s> (great statement), the word 'tat' (That) indicates — through <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification) — consciousness unconditioned by <s>ajñāna</s>, just as words like 'infinite' and 'truth' [do]. The subsidiary distinctions [among these views] should be worked out by the reader.

body.text: nanu, vastuni vikalpāsambhavāt kathaṃ parasparaviruddhamataprāmāṇyam, tasmāt kim atra heyaṃ kim upādeyam iti cet, ka evam āha vastuni vikalpo na sambhavatīti / sthāṇur vā puruṣo vā rākṣaso vā ityādivikalpasya vastuny api darśanāt / atāttvikī sā kalpanā puruṣabuddhimātraprabhavā, iyaṃ tu śāstrīyā jīveśvaravibhāgādivyavasthā iti cet, nūnam atimedhāvī bhavān /
body.translated_text: Objection: Since alternative views are impossible regarding a [single] reality, how can mutually contradictory doctrines all be valid? Therefore, what here is to be rejected and what accepted? Reply: Who says that alternative views regarding reality are impossible? For we observe alternatives such as 'Is it a post, or a person, or a demon?' even regarding a real [object]. If [you say]: 'That imagination is unreal, born merely of human intellect, whereas this differentiation of <s>jīva</s> and <s>Īśvara</s> etc. is scriptural' — then surely you are exceedingly intelligent [said ironically]!

body.text: advitīyātmatattvaṃ hi pradhānaṃ phalavattvād ajñātatvāc ca prameyaṃ śāstrasya / jīveśvaravibhāgādikalpanās tu puruṣabuddhimātraprabhavā api śāstreṇānūdyante, tattvajñānopayogitvāt / phalavat sannidhāv aphalaṃ tadaṅgam iti nyāyāt bhramasiddhasyāpi śrutyānuvādasambhavāt / etena dvaitajñānenādvaitajñānasya bādho nirastaḥ / ghaṭādidvaitajñānayos samānāśrayaviṣayatvaniyamāt, jaḍe ca pramāṇaprayojanayor abhāvenājñānānanṅgīkārāt, tadavacchinnacaitanyājñānād eva tatrāpy ajñānavyavahāropapatteḥ, prāmāṇyasya cājñātajñāpakarūpakatvāt / anyathā smṛter api tadāpatter iti / vedānteṣu sarvatra evaṃvidhavirodhe 'yam eva parihāraḥ / tadāhur vārtikakārapādāḥ (BAUBhV I.4.402)
body.translated_text: For the non-dual reality of the <s>Ātman</s> (<s>advitīya-ātma-tattva</s>) is the principal subject matter of scripture, since it is fruitful [for liberation] and is the [true] object to be known. The conceptual constructions of the <s>jīva-Īśvara</s> differentiation etc., though born merely of human intellect, are reiterated by scripture because they are useful for the knowledge of the truth. By the principle that 'in the presence of the fruitful, the fruitless is its accessory,' even what is established through error can be restated by scripture. By this, the objection that dualistic knowledge would sublate non-dual knowledge is refuted. For there is no rule that dualistic knowledge and knowledge of a pot etc. must have the same locus and object; and since in inert [objects] there is no [need for a separate] means of knowledge or purpose, <s>ajñāna</s> [regarding them] need not be separately acknowledged — since the usage of 'ignorance' regarding them is explained by the <s>ajñāna</s> delimited to the consciousness [associated with them]; and since the validity [of knowledge] consists in making known what was previously unknown. Otherwise, even memory would be liable to [count as valid knowledge]. In all of <s>Vedānta</s>, wherever such a conflict [between doctrines] arises, this is the resolution. As the revered author of the <s>Vārttika</s> says (BAUBhV I.4.402):

children.text: yayā yayā bhavet puṃsāṃ vyutpattiḥ pratyagātmani /
children.translated_text: Whatever method leads people

children.text: sā saiva prakriyā jñeeyā sādhvī sā ca vyavasthā // iti //
children.translated_text: to the understanding of the inner Self — that method alone is to be known as valid, and that is the [correct] determination.

body.text: śrutitātparyaviṣayībhūtārthaviruddhatvaṃ ca heyam eveti śataśa udghoṣitam asmābhiḥ / tasmān na kiñcid etat /
body.translated_text: And that which contradicts the meaning that is the purport of <s>śruti</s> (scripture) is indeed to be rejected — this has been proclaimed by us hundreds of times. Therefore, there is no [force to] this [objection].

body.text: nanu bhavaty avidyāvaśāj jīveśvarādivibhāgavyavasthā mānameyādipratikarmavyavasthā katham iti cet, ucyate / dṛṣyatvād vināśitvāc ca paricchinnāpy avidyānirvacanīyatvena vicārāsahā āvaraṇavikṣepaśaktidvayavatī sarvagataṃ cidātmānam āvṛṇoti, aṅgulir iva nayanapuraḥsthitā sūryamaṇḍalam / tatra cakṣuṣa evāvaraṇe 'ṇguler apy abhānaprasaṅgāt / adhiṣṭhānāvaraṇam antareṇa ca vikṣepānupapatteś ca / tataḥ sā pūrvapūrvasaṃskārajīvakarmaprayuktā satī nikhilajagadākāreṇa pariṇamate / sā ca svagatacidābhāsadvārā cittādātmyāpanneti tatkāryam api sarvam ābhāsadvārā cidanusyūtam eva / tathā ca caitanyasya dīpavatsvasambaddhasarvabhāsakatvāj jagadupādānacaitanyaṃ pramāṇāpekṣām antareṇaiva sarvadā sarvaṃ bhāsayat sarvajñaṃ bhavati / tena tatra na mānameyādivyavasthā / kin tu jīve tasya buddhyavacchinnatvena paricchinnatvāt tena cidabhivyaktiyogyena yenāntaḥkaraṇena yadā yatsambaddhaṃ bhavati tad eva tadā tadavacchinno jīvo 'nubhavatīti na sāṅkaryaprasaṅgaḥ /
body.translated_text: Objection: Granted that the differentiation of <s>jīva</s>, <s>Īśvara</s>, etc. is established through <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) — but how is the arrangement of <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge), <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge), etc. established? Reply: <s>Avidyā</s>, though limited — because it is perceived and perishable — is indescribable (<s>anirvacanīya</s>) and cannot withstand analysis, yet possessing the two powers of concealment (<s>āvaraṇa</s>) and projection (<s>vikṣepa</s>), it conceals the all-pervading conscious Self — just as a finger placed before the eye [conceals] the solar disc. For if it were the concealment of the eye itself [by the finger], then the finger too should become invisible. And without the concealment of the substratum, projection would be impossible. Then, prompted by the <s>karmas</s> of the <s>jīva</s> with accumulated impressions from previous [lives], that [<s>avidyā</s>] transforms itself into the form of the entire world. And since it, through the reflection of consciousness (<s>cidābhāsa</s>) present within it, assumes identity with the mind (<s>citta</s>) etc., its entire effect too is pervaded by consciousness through that reflection. And thus, consciousness — which, like a lamp, illuminates all that is connected with it — being the material cause of the world, illuminates everything at all times without depending on any means of knowledge, and is therefore omniscient. Hence, with respect to [Brahman], there is no arrangement of <s>pramāṇa</s>, <s>prameya</s>, etc. But in the case of the <s>jīva</s>, since [consciousness] is limited by being delimited by the <s>buddhi</s>, the <s>jīva</s> — delimited by that <s>antaḥkaraṇa</s> which is capable of manifesting consciousness — experiences only that with which it is connected at a given time. Hence there is no danger of confusion.

body.text: evam atra prakriyā -- śarīramadhye sthitaḥ sarvaśarīravyāpakaḥ sattvaprādhānyena sūkṣmapañcabhūtārabdhaḥ antaḥkaraṇākhyo 'vidyāvivarto darpaṇādivad atisvaccho netrādidvārā nirgatya yogyān ghaṭādīn viṣayān vyāpya tattadākāro bhavati drutatāmrādivat / tasya ca saurālokādivat jhaṭitye eva sa.kocavikāsāv upapadyete / sa ca sāvayavatvāt pariṇamamāno dehābhyantare ghaṭādau ca samyagvyāpya dehaghaṭayor madhye 'pi cakṣurvad avicchinno 'py avatiṣṭhate / tatra dehāvacchinnāntaḥkaraṇabhāgo 'haṅkārākhyaḥ kartety ucyate / dehaviṣayamadhyavartī daṇḍāyamānas tadbhāgo vṛttijñānākhyaḥ kriyety ucyate / viṣayavyāpakas tadbhāgo viṣayasya jñānakarmatvasampādakam abhivyaktiyogyatvam ity ucyate / tasya ca tribhāgasyāntaḥkaraṇasyātisvacchatvāt caitanyaṃ tatrābhivyajyate / tasya cābhivyaktasya caitanyasya ekatve 'pi abhivyañjakāntaḥkaraṇabhāgabhedāt tridhā vyapadeśo bhavati / kartṛbhāgāvacchinnacidaṃśaḥ pramātā, kriyābhāgāvacchinnacidaṃśaḥ pramāṇam, viṣayagatābhivyaktiyogyatvabhāgāvacchinnacidaṃśaḥ pramitir iti /
body.translated_text: The procedure here is as follows: Situated within the body, pervading the entire body, predominantly <s>sattva</s> in nature, composed of the subtle five elements — the transformation of <s>avidyā</s> called the <s>antaḥkaraṇa</s> (inner organ) is extremely transparent like a mirror etc. Going out through the eyes and other [sense organs], it pervades the appropriate objects such as a pot and takes on their respective forms, like molten copper etc. And just as with sunlight etc., its contraction and expansion occur instantaneously. And being possessed of parts, it transforms itself while pervading both the inside of the body and [external objects like] pots etc., and remains uninterrupted even in the space between the body and the pot, like the eye [remains connected to its object through its visual ray]. There, the portion of the <s>antaḥkaraṇa</s> delimited by the body is called <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (ego) and is termed the 'knower' (<s>kartā</s>). The portion that extends between the body and the object, like a rod, is called <s>vṛtti-jñāna</s> (cognitive modification) and is termed 'the activity' (<s>kriyā</s>). The portion that pervades the object produces the object's fitness for manifestation (<s>abhivyakti-yogyatva</s>) and is called 'knowledge of the object' (<s>jñāna-karmatva</s>). Because the <s>antaḥkaraṇa</s> with its three portions is extremely transparent, consciousness is manifested in it. Though the manifested consciousness is one, due to the difference in the portions of the manifesting <s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>, it receives a threefold designation: the consciousness-aspect delimited by the knower-portion is the <s>pramātṛ</s> (knower); the consciousness-aspect delimited by the activity-portion is the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge); the consciousness-aspect delimited by the portion [relating to] the fitness-for-manifestation in the object is the <s>pramiti</s> (resultant knowledge).

body.text: prameyaṃ tu viṣayagataṃ brahmacaitanyam evājñātam / tad eva jñātaṃ sat, phalam /
body.translated_text: The <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge) is the <s>Brahma</s>-consciousness present in the object that was [previously] unknown. That very [consciousness], when known, constitutes the fruit [of knowledge].

body.text: atra ca yasmin pakṣe antaḥkaraṇāvacchinno jīvaḥ, yasmiṃś ca pakṣe sarvagato 'saṅgo 'vidyāpratibimbo jīvaḥ, tatrobhayatrāpi pramātṛcaitanyoparāgārthā viṣayagatacaitanyāvaraṇabhaṅgārthā cāntaḥkaraṇavṛttiḥ / yasmiṃś ca pakṣe avidyāvacchinnaḥ sarvagato jīvaḥ āvṛttaḥ tasmin pakṣe jīvasyaiva jagadupādānatvena sarvasambaddhatvāt āvaraṇabhaṅgārthā vṛttir iti vivekaḥ /
body.translated_text: Now, in the position where the <s>jīva</s> is [consciousness] delimited by the <s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>, and in the position where the <s>jīva</s> is a reflection of <s>avidyā</s>, all-pervading and unattached — in both cases, the <s>antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti</s> (mental modification) serves to color the knower-consciousness and to remove the concealment of the consciousness [present] in the object. But in the position where the <s>jīva</s> is all-pervading and delimited by <s>avidyā</s> — being concealed — in that position, since the <s>jīva</s> itself is the material cause of the world and therefore connected with everything, the <s>vṛtti</s> serves only to remove the concealment. This is the distinction.

body.text: nanu ciduparāgārthā vṛttir iti pakṣe svato'ntaḥkaraṇasambaddhānāṃ dharmādharmādīnāṃ brahmaṇaś ca vṛttim antareṇa sarvadā bhānaṃ syāt / na syāt, caitanyasya tattadākāratvābhāvāt / tadabhāvaś ca svacche 'pi brahmacaitanye āvaraṇāt, anāvṛtte 'pi śuktirajatādāv asvacchatvāt, dharmādharmādau tu asvacchatvād āvṛtatvād vā / tena svacche 'py āvṛtte pramāṇavṛtyā tadākāratā, anāvṛte svacche tu sukhaduḥkhādau svata iti nāntaḥkaraṇasambandhamātreṇa bhānaprasaṅgaḥ /
body.translated_text: Objection: In the position where the <s>vṛtti</s> serves to color consciousness, wouldn't <s>dharma</s> (merit), <s>adharma</s> (demerit), etc. — which are inherently connected with the <s>antaḥkaraṇa</s> — and <s>Brahman</s> as well, be always manifest without [need of] a <s>vṛtti</s>? Reply: No, because consciousness does not [automatically] take on their respective forms. And the absence of such form-taking [occurs] because: in <s>Brahma</s>-consciousness, though transparent, there is concealment (<s>āvaraṇa</s>); in unconcealed [objects] like shell-silver etc., there is lack of transparency; and in <s>dharma</s>, <s>adharma</s>, etc., either because of lack of transparency or because of concealment. Therefore, when [consciousness] is transparent but concealed, the form-taking occurs through the <s>vṛtti</s> as a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge); when unconcealed and transparent, as in [the case of] pleasure, pain, etc., [the manifestation occurs] spontaneously. Hence, mere connection with the <s>antaḥkaraṇa</s> does not entail [automatic] manifestation.

body.text: nanu, brahmaṇaḥ katham āvaraṇam, niravadyasvaprakāśatvena sarvajñatvāt / satyam, svasambaddhasarvabhāsakatayā sarvajñam api antaḥkaraṇāvacchinnajīvājñānaviṣayatayā āvṛtam iti vyapadeśāt / tasmād brahma jagadupādānam iti pakṣe ciduparāgārthā āvaraṇabhaṅgārthā ca vṛttiḥ, jīvopādānatvapakṣe tu āvaraṇabhaṅgārthaiveti /
body.translated_text: Objection: How can there be concealment of <s>Brahman</s>, given that it is self-luminous without defect and therefore omniscient? Reply: True. Though omniscient by virtue of illuminating everything connected with it, it is spoken of as 'concealed' insofar as it is the object of the <s>ajñāna</s> of the <s>jīva</s> delimited by the <s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>. Therefore, in the position that <s>Brahman</s> is the material cause of the world, the <s>vṛtti</s> serves both to color consciousness and to remove the concealment; in the position that the <s>jīva</s> is the material cause, the <s>vṛtti</s> serves only to remove the concealment.

body.text: nanu, ekenaiva ghaṭādijñānenāvaraṇabhaṅge sadyo mokṣaprasaṅgaḥ, ajñānasyaikatvāt / nānājñānapakṣe 'pi ekasya jīvasyaikāñānopādhitvāt /
body.translated_text: Objection: If <s>ajñāna</s> is one, then by a single cognition of a pot etc., the concealment would be removed and immediate liberation would follow. And even in the position of multiple <s>ajñānas</s>, since one <s>jīva</s> has one <s>ajñāna</s> as its limiting condition [the same problem arises].

body.text: na, uttejakena maṇer iva vṛtyāvaraṇasyābhibhavāṅgīkārāt / tathā ca pramāṇajanyāntaḥkaraṇavṛttyabhāvasahakṛtam ajñānaṃ sati bhāty api vastuni nāsti na bhāti iti pratītijananasamartham āvaraṇam ity ucyate / vṛttau jātāyāṃ tv avacchedakābhāvād vidyamānam apy avidyamānasamam eveti na svakāryasamartham ajñānaṃ tenābhibhūtam ity ucyate /
body.translated_text: No [this is not so], because the overpowering of the concealment by the mental modification (<s>vṛtti</s>) is accepted, just as a gem [overcomes darkness] by its stimulating agent. And thus, ignorance (<s>ajñāna</s>), cooperating with the absence of a mental modification produced by a valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), is called concealment (<s>āvaraṇa</s>) — capable of producing the cognition 'it does not exist' and 'it does not appear,' even when the object is present. But when the [mental] modification has arisen, ignorance, though still existing, is equivalent to non-existence due to the absence of a delimiting [condition], and thus is not capable of producing its own effect — this is said to be 'overpowered.'

body.text: nanu, evaṃ sati brahmajñānenāpy avidyāyā anivṛtter anirmokṣaprasaṅgaḥ / na, tattvamasyādivākyārthajñānād avidyānivṛttyabhyupagamāt, svaviṣayapramātvenaivāvidyānivartakatvān mahāvākyārthaj,jānasyaivābādhitaviṣayatayā pramātvāt / pratyakṣādīnāṃ tu bādhitaviṣayatayā bhramatve 'pi vyavahārasāmarthyena prāmāṇyābhimānāt, jñānādajñānanivṛtter anyatrādarśanaṃ cākiñcitkaram, svānubhavasiddhatvāt, anyathānupapatteś ca sarvato balavattvāt / taduktam (Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādyam 1)
body.translated_text: Objection: If so, since <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) would not be removed even by the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>, there would be the unwanted consequence of non-liberation (<s>anirmokṣa</s>). No, because the removal of <s>avidyā</s> by the knowledge of the meaning of the great sentences (<s>mahāvākya</s>) such as '<s>tat tvam asi</s>' (You are That) is accepted. The knowledge of the meaning of the great sentences alone is the remover of <s>avidyā</s>, since it alone has the status of valid knowledge (<s>pramātva</s>) regarding its own subject matter, and its object is not sublated (<s>abādhita</s>). But perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) and other [means of knowledge], though erroneous since their objects are sublated, are regarded as valid due to their capacity for practical dealings (<s>vyavahāra</s>). And the non-observation elsewhere [of knowledge removing ignorance] is inconsequential, because it is established by one's own experience, and because the principle of 'no other explanation' (<s>anyathānupapatti</s>) is stronger than everything else. As it is said (<s>Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya</s> 1):

children.text: anyathānupapatiś ced asti vastuprasādhikā /
children.translated_text: If the principle of 'no other explanation' (<s>anyathānupapatti</s>) establishes reality,

children.text: pinaṣṭhyasṛṣtivaimatyaṃ saiva sarvabalādhikā // iti //
children.translated_text: then it alone, being stronger than all else, crushes the dispute about non-creation.

body.text: atha vā mūlājñānasyaivāvasthājñānāni ghaṭādiviṣayāvaraṇāni / ajñānasya prāgabhāvasthānīyatvena yāvanti jñānāni tāvanty ajñānānīty abhyupagamāt ekena ca jñānenaikājñānasyaiva nāśāt, ghaṭādijñānenāvaraṇanāśe 'pi na kācid anupapattiḥ /
body.translated_text: Alternatively, root ignorance (<s>mūlājñāna</s>) itself constitutes the state-specific ignorances, the concealments regarding objects such as pots. Since it is accepted that there are as many ignorances as there are cognitions — <s>ajñāna</s> occupying the place of prior non-existence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>) — and since by one cognition only one ignorance is destroyed, there is no difficulty even when the concealment is removed by cognition of a pot and so forth.

body.text: nanu, anumānādihir āvaraṇaṃ nivartate na vā / ādye sākṣātkāribhramasyāpi śaṅkhapītatvādeḥ śvetatvādyanumānādinā nivṛttiprasaṅgaḥ, adhiṣṭhānājñānopādānakatvena bhramasya tannivṛttau nivṛtteḥ / yauktikajñānena ca brahmaṇyavidyānivṛtteḥ sākṣātkārārthaṃ śravaṇamananādyapekṣaṇaṃ na syāt / dvitīye ca vahnyādivyavahāro na syāt, pratibandhakasya vidyamānatvāt / ucyate -- dvividham āvaraṇam, ekam asattvāpādakam antaḥkaraṇāvacchinnasākṣiniṣṭham, anyad abhānāpādakaṃ viṣayāvacchinnabrahmacaitanyaniṣṭhaṃ, ghaṭam ahaṃ na jānāmīty ubhayāvacchedānubhavāt / tatrādyaṃ parokṣāparokṣasādhāraṇapramāmātreṇa nivartate / anumite 'pi vahnyādau nāstīti pratyayānudayāt / dvitīyaṃ tu sākṣātkāreṇaiva nivartate / yanniṣṭhaṃ yadākāraṃ jñānaṃ tanniṣṭhaṃ tadākāram ajñānaṃ nāśayatīti niyamāt, parokṣāparokṣaniṣṭhatvāt / tad uktam (Pañca 7.45)
body.translated_text: Objection: Does inference and so forth remove the concealment or not? In the first case, there would be the unwanted consequence that even directly perceived error — such as yellowness of a conch-shell — would be removed by inference of whiteness, since error, having ignorance of the substratum as its material cause, is removed when that [ignorance] is removed. And since <s>avidyā</s> regarding <s>Brahman</s> would be removed by logical knowledge, the need for hearing (<s>śravaṇa</s>), reflection (<s>manana</s>), and so forth for the sake of direct realization (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>) would not arise. In the second case, practical dealings such as those regarding fire would not be possible, since the obstruction [of ignorance] would still exist. Reply: Concealment (<s>āvaraṇa</s>) is of two kinds — one that makes [the object appear as] non-existent (<s>asattvāpādaka</s>), residing in the <s>sākṣin</s> (witness-consciousness) as delimited by the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>); and another that causes non-manifestation (<s>abhānāpādaka</s>), residing in the <s>Brahman</s>-consciousness as delimited by the object — as experienced in both delimitations in the cognition 'I do not know the pot.' Of these, the first is removed by any valid cognition, whether mediate (<s>parokṣa</s>) or immediate (<s>aparokṣa</s>), since even with regard to inferred fire and so forth, the cognition 'it does not exist' does not arise. The second, however, is removed only by direct realization (<s>sākṣātkāra</s>), because of the rule that a cognition residing in X and having the form of Y destroys ignorance residing in X and having the form of Y — and because it can be either mediate or immediate. As stated (<s>Pañcapādikā</s> 7.45):

children.text: parokṣajñānato naśyed asattvāvṛttihetutā /
children.translated_text: Through mediate knowledge (<s>parokṣajñāna</s>), the cause of the concealment producing [the appearance of] non-existence is destroyed;

children.text: aparokṣadhiyā naśyed abhānāvṛttihetutā //
children.translated_text: Through immediate knowledge (<s>aparokṣadhī</s>), the cause of the concealment producing non-manifestation is destroyed.

body.text: tenānumānāder asattvāvaraṇanāśāt tatra tadvyavahāraḥ / abhānāvaraṇanivṛttyā ca sopādhikasākṣātkāribhramanivṛttir iti / tasmān nirdharmakasyāpy ātmano 'vidyāntaḥkaraṇatādātmyādhyāsāt taddharmakartṛtvabhoktṛtvādyadhyāsa upapadyate /
body.translated_text: Therefore, from the destruction by inference and so forth of the non-existence concealment, practical dealings (<s>vyavahāra</s>) regarding that [object] become possible. And from the removal of the non-manifestation concealment, conditioned direct-perceptual error is also removed. Thus, even for the <s>ātman</s> (Self) that is devoid of attributes (<s>nirdharmaka</s>), the superimposition (<s>adhyāsa</s>) of agency (<s>kartṛtva</s>), enjoyership (<s>bhoktṛtva</s>), and so forth is explained through the superimposition of identity between <s>avidyā</s>, the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>), and [the Self], and from the attributes thereof.

body.text: nanu tvanmate 'nirvacanīyakhyātyabhyupagamāt, ye kartṛtvādayo 'ntaḥkaraṇadharmā ātmany adhyasyante te 'nirvacanīyās tatrotpadyanta iti vaktavyam / tathā ca vyāvahārikaprātītikabhedena kartṛtvabhoktṛtvādīnāṃ dvedhāvabhāsaḥ syāt / na syāt, tādātmyābhimānenāvivekāt / sakaladharmaviśiṣṭasyaivāntaḥkaraṇasyātmany adhyastatvena dvayābhāvād vā / tasmād ekasyaivātmana upādhibhedena pramātrādivyavasthopapatter na saugatamatāpattir na vā virodhaḥ / anyāpi vyavasthāḥ spaṣṭataram upariṣṭād upapādayiṣyante / tasmāj jñānasvarūpasyātmanaḥ suṣuptāv avyabhicārād dehendriyādīnāṃ ca vyabhicārād dṛśyatvāc ca tatra tatrātmabuddhis teṣāṃ teṣāṃ vādināṃ bhrāntir ity aupaniṣadamatam eva pramāṇam iti siddham // 1 //
body.translated_text: Objection: In your view, since the doctrine of the indescribable (<s>anirvacanīya</s>) error is accepted, the agency and other attributes of the inner organ that are superimposed on the <s>ātman</s> must be called indescribable (<s>anirvacanīya</s>), as they arise there [in superimposition].
